wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e111.summary: Taking from the previous question the supposition that by divine power many purely theological truths can be evidently known, asks whether evident knowledge of them is scientia proprie dicta.
claims: By divine power many purely theological truths can be evidently known (supposed from q1).

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e131.summary: First argument for no: all strict science is through a cause (Posterior Analytics I: to know is to know a thing through its cause), but nothing predicable of God, being really God, has a cause.
claims: Strict science is knowledge through a cause (argument).
Nothing predicable of God has a cause (argument).

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e144.summary: Second and third arguments. Strict science is the effect of demonstration, whose middle is a definition, and God, being simply simple, has no definition, so nothing can be demonstrated or scientifically known of him. Also, every scientifically known proposition is second-mode per se, predicating a property of a subject, but God has no property, since a property is really distinct from its subject.
claims: The middle of demonstration is a definition (argument).
God has no definition (argument).
A property is really distinct from its subject (argument).

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e168.summary: Argument to the contrary: if not, it would only be because of the identity of predicate and subject. That is no obstacle, since there is strict science of being (metaphysics), yet nothing really differs from being, or it would be non-being.
claims: There is strict science of being though nothing differs from being.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e180.summary: Sets out the plan: first, which proposition is known by strict science; second, what strict science is; third, the question.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e187.summary: Defines the proposition knowable by strict science: a necessary, doubtable proposition apt to be made evident through necessary propositions evidently applied to it by syllogistic discourse.
claims: A strictly knowable proposition is necessary, doubtable, and apt to be made evident by syllogism from evident necessary propositions.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e198.summary: The first condition, necessity, excludes contingent propositions: though evidently knowable, they can be false and so are not strictly scientifically knowable.
claims: Contingent propositions are not strictly knowable even when evident.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e209.summary: The second condition, being doubtable, excludes self-evident propositions, which though necessary and evident are not doubtable. Grosseteste on Posterior Analytics I confirms: knowledge of principles is not acquired by teaching, since we learn only what at first seems doubtful or false and then is made manifest. So every knowable conclusion is first doubtful or apparently false and then made evident through principles.
claims: Self-evident propositions are not strictly knowable because they are not doubtable.
We learn only what at first seems doubtful or false.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e240.summary: Clarifies: it is not required that a strictly knowable proposition actually be doubtful or seem false to every learner, only that it can be doubted by someone or seem false and then be made known by syllogism. This distinguishes it from self-evident propositions and first principles.
claims: Dubitability means possible doubt, not actual doubt for every learner.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e258.summary: Further support from Posterior Analytics II: questions equal in number what we truly know, so everything knowable is open to question, and everything open to question is doubtable.
claims: Everything knowable can be asked about, and so is doubtable.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e277.summary: The third condition, aptness to be made evident through evident propositions by syllogistic discourse, distinguishes the knowable from first principles that are not self-evident and hence doubtable, but cannot be made known by syllogism. Example: 'heat is calefactive' is necessary and doubtable. Someone who intuited heat by intellect alone, never felt it or saw it heat (nothing heatable being near), could doubt whether heat produces heat, as whether whiteness produces whiteness. Yet no syllogism can make it evident; only experience through intuitive cognition can. So it is not strictly knowable.
claims: Some first principles are not self-evident but are doubtable.
'Heat is calefactive' becomes evident only through experience, not syllogism.
Such experiential principles are not strictly knowable by scientia.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e323.summary: First objection to the second condition: some self-evident proposition is demonstrable and so strictly knowable but not doubtable. Alhazen in his Perspectiva (I.3) demonstrates 'the whole is greater than its part', which is self-evident.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e341.summary: Second objection: every property is demonstrable of its subject, and some such proposition is self-evident and so not doubtable. Also, every necessary complex posterior to the first principle is demonstrable through it, since a syllogism from it is from true, first and immediate premises, yet some such complexes are self-evident.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e361.summary: Third objection: if every strictly knowable proposition is doubtable, an intellect that cannot doubt or err, such as God's, could know nothing by strict science. That is false, since strict science implies no imperfection and so should not be denied of the divine intellect.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e381.summary: Objection that the third condition is superfluous: every necessary non-self-evident proposition, and only such, is strictly knowable, and every such proposition is doubtable, so doubtability suffices. The major is supported by Posterior Analytics I: we know principles insofar as we know the terms, so no principle is doubtable, and every necessary proposition is a principle or a knowable conclusion.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e416.summary: Further support from Topics I: demonstration is from first and true immediate premises, or from what has gained credence through such premises. So every demonstration rests on self-evident propositions, every principle that is not also a conclusion is self-evident, and none is doubtable.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e433.summary: Answers the first objection by distinguishing senses of 'demonstration'. Most broadly and improperly, any syllogism from necessary premises, so a syllogism concluding a self-evident proposition from non-self-evident necessary premises can be called demonstration, since it is neither sophistical nor dialectical. Broadly, any syllogism from necessary and prior premises, whether the conclusion is self-evident or not. Strictly and properly, a syllogism producing knowledge from necessary premises apt to cause knowledge of the conclusion; this is how Aristotle, the doctors and the expositors speak.
claims: 'Demonstration' has a broadest, a broad, and a strict sense.
In the strict sense, a demonstration's premises must be apt to cause knowledge of the conclusion.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e472.summary: So a self-evident proposition is demonstrable in the first two senses, perhaps Alhazen's meaning, but not in the strict sense. A self-evident proposition is known precisely from knowledge of its terms, or it would not be self-evident, so its knowledge is not apt to be caused by premises and it is not demonstrable or strictly knowable.
claims: A self-evident proposition is not strictly demonstrable, since it is known from its terms.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e490.summary: Objection: though a self-evident proposition can be known from its terms, if knowledge of the terms did not suffice, the premises would cause knowledge of it, so the premises are apt to cause it and it is demonstrable.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e506.summary: Reply: by that reasoning even the first principle could be demonstrated, since if knowledge of the terms did not suffice one could syllogize it from some known propositions.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e517.summary: Answers the objection that if the first principle were unknown nothing would be known: sometimes something is actually known while the first principle is not, so the argument stands. Ockham concludes that it belongs to a knowable proposition that its knowledge can be caused by knowledge of principles, and so it is doubtable. By the counterfactual reasoning, it is knowable in exactly the way it is doubtable: if knowledge of terms did not suffice, it could be doubted, for instance if apprehended without the premises from which it should be known.
claims: Something can be actually known while the first principle is not actually known.
A proposition is knowable exactly insofar as it is doubtable.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e552.summary: Answers the second objection: not every property is demonstrable of its subject. Some can be known to belong only by experience, never by demonstration, and this is true not only of self-evident propositions but often of non-self-evident ones such as 'heat is calefactive'.
claims: Not every property is demonstrable of its subject.
Some properties are known to belong only by experience.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e569.summary: Answers the second part: a necessary complex posterior to the first principle is not always demonstrable through it, even if it can be syllogistically inferred from it. It is also required that knowledge of the principle can cause knowledge of the posterior, which is lacking here.
claims: Syllogistic inferability is insufficient for demonstrability; causal dependence of knowledge is required.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e582.summary: Answers the third objection: Ockham concedes that the divine intellect lacks science in this strict sense. Such science is not a pure perfection but includes the imperfection of being apt to be produced by other complex knowledge.
claims: God does not have scientia in the strict sense.
Strict science includes the imperfection of being produced by other knowledge.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e591.summary: Answers the objection against the third condition: it is not superfluous, because not every non-self-evident proposition is strictly knowable. There are many first, indemonstrable, immediate principles that are not self-evident.
claims: There are many first indemonstrable principles that are not self-evident.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e604.summary: Some conclusions are demonstrable through self-evident principles, with ultimate resolution to them; others resolve to principles known only by experience ('heat is calefactive', 'heaviness inclines downward'), which are first but doubtable. This is Augustine's meaning in Retractationes I.8 on which arts the soul 'brought with it': those whose resolution ends in self-evident principles can be drawn out by ordered questioning without experience, as a teacher proposes principles and then conclusions in order. Others, like medicine and astrology that pertain to the bodily senses, cannot be learned without experience, though opinion or belief about them can be acquired by teaching. Augustine says the same in De Trinitate. Aristotle agrees (Metaphysics I, Posterior Analytics II): from sense comes memory, from memory experience, from experience the universal that is the principle of art and science. Such first propositions predicate a property of a subject and are doubtable: art arises when from many experiences one universal judgment is formed, that this remedy helped Callias and Socrates with this illness, and so all phlegmatic or bilious patients. So experiential first principles are doubtable and not self-evident.
claims: Some sciences resolve to self-evident principles, others to principles known only by experience.
Arts resolving to self-evident principles can be elicited by ordered questioning.
Arts like medicine cannot be acquired without experience.
Universal principles of art and science arise from sense, memory and experience.
Experiential first principles are doubtable and not self-evident.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e747.summary: Further confirmation from Ethics I.7: some principles are grasped by induction, some by sense, some by habituation, others otherwise, with the Commentator agreeing.
claims: Principles are acquired in diverse ways: induction, sense, habituation.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e756.summary: Answers the authority of Posterior Analytics I in two ways: it speaks of self-evident principles; or, universally, that principles are known when the terms are known, excluding prior propositions from which they could be inferred, though not any knowledge of terms suffices. Self-evident propositions need any knowledge of terms, intuitive or abstractive. Others need intuitive knowledge of at least some term or what it imports, often many intuitions. Example: 'every herb of this species helps the feverish' cannot be syllogized but is known from intuition: one sees health follow eating the herb, removes all other causes, evidently knows that this herb caused health, and so has an experiment about a singular. Knowing that all individuals of the same kind have like effects in like patients, one evidently takes the universal as a principle. On Topics I, demonstration is from first and true premises, not necessarily from self-evident ones; first principles and self-evident principles are not the same. Second article: science, as distinguished from the other intellectual habits of Ethics VI, is evident knowledge of a necessary truth apt to be caused by premises applied to it by syllogistic discourse. 'Evident' excludes opinion, suspicion and faith; 'necessary' excludes evident knowledge of contingents; 'by syllogistic discourse' excludes first principles. 'Apt to be caused' because it can in fact be caused by experience, as one could know the moon is eclipsable by experience alone. That it is science follows from the fivefold division of truth-bearing habits. Objections: principles and conclusions are not acquired the same way, so conclusions cannot be known by experience without demonstration; and knowledge from experience and from demonstration would differ in species, more than quia and propter quid knowledge, which do.
claims: First principles need not be self-evident.
Non-self-evident principles require intuitive cognition of some term.
A singular experiment, with other causes excluded, yields evident knowledge of causation.
All individuals of the same species produce like effects in like patients.
Science is evident knowledge of a necessary truth apt to be caused by syllogistic discourse.
Scientific knowledge of a conclusion can in fact be caused by experience.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e909.summary: Confirmation of the objection: distinct causes cause distinct effects, and sciences gained by experience and by demonstration have specifically distinct causes, so they differ in species. Nor can they be different species, since in one intellect there cannot be two specifically distinct abstractive cognitions of the same complex.
claims: In one intellect there cannot be two specifically distinct abstractive cognitions of the same complex.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e929.summary: Answers the first objection: some principles and some conclusions can be acquired in the same way, but beyond that common way there is one proper to conclusions, namely demonstration, which cannot belong to first principles.
claims: Demonstration is a mode of acquisition proper to conclusions.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e942.summary: Answers the second: knowledge of a conclusion acquired by experience and by demonstration are of the same species. Specifically distinct causes can have specifically the same effect, as sun and fire each sufficiently produce heat of one species. Intuitive knowledge yielding evident knowledge of a singular contingent truth ('this herb heals this illness') is a mediate partial cause of knowing the demonstrable conclusion ('every such herb heals'). It is only partial, since evident knowledge that like individuals have like effects is also needed. Knowledge of premises is another sufficient cause of the same species. If a conclusion is first known by experience and then by demonstration, no new species of science arises, only an intensification, as wood heated by the sun and then by fire.
claims: Knowledge of a conclusion from experience and from demonstration is of the same species.
Specifically distinct causes can produce specifically the same effect.
Intuitive knowledge of singulars is a mediate partial cause of universal knowledge.
Learning a conclusion first by experience then by demonstration only intensifies the same habit.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e1007.summary: Objection: according to Posterior Analytics I, a necessary truth cannot be known through a contingent one, though it can be inferred from it, so knowledge of contingent truth contributes nothing to strict science.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e1020.summary: Reply: Aristotle means that a necessary truth cannot be demonstrated through a contingent one as a premise. But through evident knowledge of a contingent truth and knowledge of a necessary truth, not arranged in syllogistic form, evident knowledge of a demonstrable conclusion can be had. 'This herb heals, therefore every herb of this species heals' follows not by an intrinsic middle that would make a syllogism, but by an extrinsic middle: all agents of the same most specific species produce effects of the same kind.
claims: A necessary truth cannot be demonstrated through a contingent premise.
Evident knowledge of a necessary conclusion can arise from a contingent truth plus an extrinsic principle.
The inference from one herb to all herbs of the species holds by an extrinsic middle (uniformity principle).

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e1053.summary: Objection: then one experiment would suffice for a principle of art and science, since knowing of one singular that it produces such an effect would suffice, if that proposition is universally true.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e1063.summary: Further objection: then experience could yield principles only about most specific species, not genera, since 'all things of the same genus produce effects of the same kind' is simply false, as some substances produce substances and some only accidents.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e1079.summary: Further objection: 'this herb heals, so every herb of this species heals' is invalid, because some such herb might instead harm by having the contrary of what makes this one heal.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e1099.summary: Answers the first: sometimes one experiment suffices, sometimes many are needed. If the principle's subject is a most specific species, one suffices: to know 'all heat is calefactive' it suffices to know evidently that this heat heats or heated. If the subject is common to several species, an experiment about a singular of each species is required, as knowing that every act generates a habit requires experience that acts of principles and of conclusions do so. This holds when the principle is taken precisely by experience. Then the deduction rests not on 'causes of the same genus produce effects of the same kind' but on 'what belongs to each species under a genus belongs universally to the genus'. Such a principle is reached by experience and a kind of induction, inferring a universal about the genus from universals about all its species (every man, ass, lion grows, so every animal grows). That is why Aristotle says first principles are sometimes taken by induction.
claims: For a most specific species one experiment suffices for a universal principle.
For a genus, experience of each contained species is required.
Universals about a genus are inferred from universals about all its species.
First principles are sometimes acquired by induction.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e1169.summary: So to the argument: knowledge of one singular suffices for an evident proposition about a most specific species, but not about something common to several kinds.
claims: Knowledge of one singular suffices only for propositions about most specific species.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e1180.summary: Likewise to the second: a proposition about something common to several kinds is reached not by the uniformity principle about causes of the same genus but in the way just explained.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e1191.summary: Answers the third objection: 'every such herb heals this illness' is not the first proposition taken from experience, unless the herb's substance itself is the principle of healing. If some quality in the herb is the principle, the proposition predicating 'healing' of what is common to that quality is the first principle, and 'every such herb heals' is a demonstrable conclusion, as 'all heat is calefactive' is a principle and 'all fire is calefactive' a conclusion. The consequence 'this herb heals, so every such herb heals' is still valid, though its consequent is a conclusion. It holds through the evident necessary middle: whatever absolute thing or property following an absolute thing belongs to one individual can belong to every individual of the same kind. To the claim that some such herb might cause illness: it can both cause and heal the illness, since nothing prevents something being in potency to principles of contraries.
claims: If a quality is the healing principle, the proposition about that quality is the first principle.
'All fire is calefactive' is a conclusion from 'all heat is calefactive'.
Whatever belongs to one individual can belong to every individual of the same kind.
A thing can be in potency to principles of contraries.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e1255.summary: Notes that this last consequence holds according to theology and truth, though the Philosopher and those who err would deny it.
claims: The uniformity consequence holds in theology and truth, though Aristotle would deny it.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e1262.summary: Answers the first confirmation: specifically distinct causes do not always have specifically distinct effects, and multiplying prior causes does not always multiply posterior effects, since on all views many essential causes concur in producing one effect.
claims: Many essential causes can concur in one effect.
Distinct causes do not always yield distinct effects.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e1273.summary: Answers the other proof: 'science quia' and 'science propter quid' can mean the demonstrations themselves, which differ in species for the same conclusion because they have different premises (Aristotle's sense in Posterior Analytics I), or the knowledge caused by their premises, which does not differ in species, however much the premise-cognitions that efficiently cause it differ.
claims: Demonstrations quia and propter quid of the same conclusion differ in species.
Knowledge of the conclusion caused by each does not differ in species.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e1299.summary: Objection: according to the previous question, things that cannot have the same effect differ in species, and science quia, however intensified, never makes one know propter quid, so they differ in species, and likewise science from demonstration and from experience. Reply: science quia never produces knowledge propter quid because that requires another cause, knowledge of the premises of the propter quid demonstration. So it is distinct in species from knowledge of those premises.
claims: Science quia never yields knowledge propter quid without knowledge of the propter quid premises.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e1323.summary: Assesses this: the opinion that science acquired by experience and by demonstration is the same is most probable if knowledge of the conclusion is really and wholly distinct from knowledge of the principles. Otherwise it would have no probability.
claims: The identity of experiential and demonstrative knowledge is probable only if conclusion-knowledge is really distinct from principle-knowledge.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e1336.summary: Third article: opinions on the question. The first opinion holds that however certain and evident knowledge of necessary theological truths might be, it is not strict science. All strict science is acquired through the cause of what is concluded of the subject, and nothing predicable of God has a cause (Posterior Analytics I: we know when we know the cause by which the thing is). It raises the reply that Aristotle means a complex cause, not an incomplex one.
claims: Strict science is through the cause of what is concluded (reported).
Nothing predicable of God has a cause (reported).

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e1363.summary: The opinion replies that Aristotle explicitly speaks of the cause by which the thing is, not by which the complex is, and in Posterior Analytics II and Physics I he illustrates with the four causes of things. Further: every subject of science is caused and composite, having composite quidditative and denominative concepts; has a property really different from it; and has a property demonstrable through its definition. None of these fit God. Still, something can be concluded of God a priori, but it is not strict science because it is not through a real cause.
claims: Aristotle's 'cause' is a real cause of the thing, not of the complex (reported).
Every subject of science is caused, composite, and has a really distinct property (reported).
Something can be concluded of God a priori without strict science (reported).

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e1405.summary: Ockham objects that the two claims are inconsistent. When a conclusion is known a priori, there is a truth-bearing habit of it. It is not understanding, which concerns only principles, self-evident or known by experience. It is not wisdom, which covers principles and conclusions. It is not art or prudence, which concern doables and makeables. So it is science. The opinion might reply that such knowledge is wisdom, like metaphysics of being, because it is not through a cause.
claims: A priori knowledge of a conclusion must be science by elimination of the other intellectual habits.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e1427.summary: Counter: a proposition concluded through something prior but not through a prior real cause can be found among lower things. On their own view, as God's indivisibility can be shown from his infinity, the incorruptibility or simplicity of the intellective soul can be shown from its intellectuality. That habit is not wisdom, since it is not about universal first causes, nor understanding, art or prudence, so it is strict science without a real cause.
claims: Some strict science of creatures proceeds through prior concepts without a real cause.
The soul's incorruptibility can be shown from its intellectuality (on their view).

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e1451.summary: Reports a second opinion (Scotus's): there can be strict propter quid, a priori science of such truths. It shows this first for essential perfections demonstrated of the essence, second for notionals, third for relations ad extra.
claims: Theological truths admit propter quid a priori science (reported).

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e1464.summary: First point of the opinion: there is an order among the rationes under which God is conceivable. The ratio of essence is first, and others are prior or posterior according to their nearness to it. Whatever order things would have if really distinct, they have a like order of reason where distinct by reason. If essential perfections were really distinct (perfect intellectual nature, perfect intellect, the representing ratio of the object, the act of understanding the primary object, then the act about secondary objects), there would be a real order among them, and propositions like 'whatever has perfect immaterial nature has perfect intellectuality' and 'a perfect intellect with its object present understands unless impeded' would be propter quid. Similarly for will and willing.
claims: The rationes under which God is conceived are ordered with essence first (reported).
What would have a real order if really distinct has a like order of reason (reported).
Propositions linking divine nature, intellect and act are propter quid (reported).

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e1536.summary: Second point: if memory (including intellect and present object), the act of intelligence, the act of expressing declarative knowledge (dicere), and the produced word were really distinct, there would be a real order, memory first, saying second, word third, and likewise for will and spiration of the Holy Spirit. So posterior notionals could be known through prior ones as propter quid causes. A further argument: demonstrations quia and propter quid of the same thing run in opposite orders. Quia concludes first what is nearer the effect, while propter quid concludes first what is nearer the first cause. Some things can be concluded of God from effects and some cannot, so they are not equally immediate to God and inhere in a natural order.
claims: Divine notionals (memory, saying, word) have an order of reason (reported).
Quia and propter quid demonstrations run in opposite orders (reported).
Some divine attributes are knowable from effects and some not, showing an order (reported).

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e1592.summary: Confirmation: some things can be known of God by a confused concept, others only by a distinct one.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e1599.summary: Third point (from his Quodlibet): 'God is omnipotent', and likewise 'creative', 'beatificative', are demonstrable as mediated necessary truths. Whatever real order things would have if really distinct, they have the same order of knowability however distinct. If nature, intellect, will and power ad extra were really distinct, power would follow because the nature has such intellect and will, so the order of knowability holds. Likewise the notional belongs to the essence more immediately than what is related ad extra, and comparing it to a divine person there can be a true middle.
claims: Omnipotence is demonstrable of God through intellect and will (reported).
Relations ad extra are posterior to the notionals (reported).

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e1643.summary: Further argument: there can be strict science of any quiddity not contained in a prior composite, having a per se definition, cause and really distinct property, and having several denominative second-mode concepts. That is not because of composition, causation or a really distinct property, as being shows, but precisely because it has several ordered concepts. God is like this.
claims: Strict science requires only several ordered concepts of a subject (reported).
Being is a subject of science without composition or cause (reported).

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e1663.summary: Ockham argues against the opinion. First, attributes cannot be demonstrated propter quid of God distinctly known. No common quidditative concept can be demonstrated propter quid of what is immediately contained under it, since that proposition is immediate (Posterior Analytics I). Every such concept is common to God and creatures (to be proved later) and quidditative, since, as will be proved, there is no real or rational distinction between the divine essence and intellect or will. So the concept of goodness or the like cannot be demonstrated of God.
claims: No common quidditative concept is demonstrable propter quid of what falls immediately under it.
Concepts of divine attributes are common to God and creatures.
There is no real or rational distinction between the divine essence and intellect or will.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e1698.summary: Possible reply: of the very same thing without any distinction there can be several concepts, quidditative and denominative.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e1705.summary: Counter: when whatever one concept expresses ex parte rei is also expressed by another, there is no more reason for one to be quidditative than the other. If there is no distinction at all between the divine essence, intellect and act, nothing imaginable is expressed by one concept that is not expressed by the other, so both are quidditative or neither. The reply that they express the same thing in different ways is raised.
claims: Concepts expressing exactly the same thing are equally quidditative.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e1724.summary: Counter: no such diversity of modes can be assigned except because of some non-identity in reality.
claims: Diversity of modes of expression requires some non-identity in reality.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e1731.summary: Confirmation: a concept is quidditative precisely because it expresses the quiddity and nothing else, so every such concept is quidditative. It is immediate, since nothing is a middle: not God, and not anything created, which is the other member of the division ('some wisdom is created, some uncreated'). Wisdom is immediately predicated of uncreated wisdom, which is not distinguished from the essence. So no such concept is demonstrable a priori of God distinctly known, except perhaps a common property of being demonstrated of God through being as middle.
claims: A concept expressing only the quiddity is quidditative.
Attributes are predicated immediately of God.
At most, properties of being in general could be demonstrated of God through being.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e1762.summary: Second, no notional can be demonstrated of the divine essence through another notional, since the only distinctions are between essence and relation and among the relations, with no distinction among one person's properties. So there is no middle to demonstrate one from another.
claims: No notional is demonstrable of the essence through another notional.
The only divine distinctions are between essence and relations and among relations.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e1778.summary: Third, by the same reasoning concepts ad extra cannot be demonstrated of the divine essence. If 'omnipotent' were demonstrable, it would be of the essence or of a person. Not of the essence: the middle would be a real thing or a being of reason. A real thing can only be the essence, a person or a relation (absent a formal distinction of attributes), but the predicate does not belong to a person or relation before the essence, since whatever belongs to a person or relation belongs to something else that is not it, so it belongs first to the essence. Not a being of reason: what is proper to a real thing is said of it before of any concept, and omnipotence is proper to a real thing. Nor of a person a priori, since then someone could know that the essence is omnipotent while doubting about the person, the opposite of which will be shown.
claims: Omnipotence cannot be demonstrated a priori of the divine essence or of a person.
What belongs to a divine person or relation and to something else belongs first to the essence.
What is proper to a real thing is predicated of it before any concept.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e1843.summary: Considers the reply that besides the essence there is a formal distinction of attributes, sufficient for one concept to be quidditative and another denominative and for propter quid a priori demonstration. Against this: it does not save the doctor, who holds that all this can be saved without formal distinction, by distinction of reason or by mutually related relations of reason. He says one thing can virtually contain quasi-denominative concepts distinguishable from the quidditative concept precisely by mutual relations of reason, though perhaps a greater distinction could be posited. So he means to posit such concepts without relation ad extra even without formal distinction.
claims: Scotus holds that quidditative and denominative concepts of God can be distinguished by relations of reason alone.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e1887.summary: Further, even granting formal distinction, one concept need not be quidditative and the other denominative. If the intellect's concept is called denominative, it is so relative either to the essence or to one thing essentially including essence, intellect and the rest. Not the latter, since what includes both equally makes neither concept more quidditative, as with matter and form in the composite. Not the former, since as with really distinct items forming a per se unity, neither concept is more denominative of the other than the reverse, and likewise for formally distinct items: neither includes the other formally. The essence-concept is not denominative of the intellect, nor the reverse. So the essence-concept would have to be quidditative of something not formally the essence, of which the intellect-concept is denominative, which is impossible since everything such includes intellect and essence equally.
claims: Even with formal distinction, there is no ground for one concept being quidditative and another denominative.
Concepts of the parts of a per se unity are equally quidditative relative to the whole.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e1973.summary: Possible reply: there is no single thing essentially including intellect and essence; the essence itself is the quiddity and the attributes are like its properties.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e1984.summary: Counter: really distinct items make a per se unity through composition, as matter and form do, so all the more formally distinct items make a per se unity through real identity. So the divine essence and intellect make a per se unity that includes intellect as essentially as essence.
claims: Formally distinct but really identical items make a per se unity.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e2000.summary: Confirmation from their own principle: what would have an order if really distinct has the same order when only formally distinct. If essence and intellect were really distinct, intellect would be posterior, yet neither would include the other essentially, and the essence-concept would be no more quidditative of the intellect than the reverse. So now too it is not, and the intellect-concept is as quidditative of the intellect as the essence-concept of the essence. Against the reply that the essence-concept is quidditative of the person while attribute-concepts are not: when items are per se ordered as first, second and third, and the first and third form a per se unity, the second does too. On their view every essential is more immediate to the essence than any notional, so if essence and relation constitute the person, the essential and relation constitute something including both, which can only be the person. So every essential is as quidditative of the person as the essence or relation.
claims: On Scotus's principle, the essence-concept is not more quidditative than the intellect-concept.
If first and third of an ordered series form a per se unity, so does the second.
Every essential attribute is as quidditative of a divine person as the essence is.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e2081.summary: Ockham's own answer begins: first, demonstration is either quia or propter quid.
claims: Demonstration is either quia or propter quid.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e2088.summary: Second: of what is predicated of God, some are things (if a thing can be predicated) and some only concepts. An intellect able to understand the divine essence can understand paternity, filiation and spiration and predicate them of the essence, since an intellect can predicate any known item of any known item, thing or concept. But such propositions are not possible for us in this state, since under the common law we cannot understand the divine essence or paternity in themselves, only in a concept. Example of the second: predicating the concept of being or wisdom in general of God ('God is a being', 'God is wise').
claims: An intellect can predicate any known item, thing or concept, of any known item.
An intellect knowing God in himself could predicate paternity of the essence.
In this state we know God only in concepts, not in himself.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e2125.summary: Third: the subject of propositions about God can be the very thing that God is, or some concept predicable of it. What this concept is and how it differs from the thing will be discussed elsewhere; here Ockham assumes it is neither really nor formally the thing it is of.
claims: A concept of God is neither really nor formally identical with God.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e2139.summary: All that is said of predicating things in divinis should be understood on the probable opinion that the act of understanding is not subject or predicate of the proposition but its object. On the other, also probable, opinion that every subject of a mental proposition is an act of understanding or a quality inhering in the mind, the proposition about the deity distinctly is composed not of the thing but of a distinct intellection of the deity, which is not possible for us. Then one should speak proportionately of that proposition as if it were composed of the thing.
claims: Both the fictum/object theory and the intellectio theory of mental propositions are probable.
On the intellectio theory, a distinct proposition about God would be composed of a distinct intellection of deity.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e2165.summary: First conclusion: nothing intrinsic to God can be demonstrated of the divine essence where the essence in itself is the subject and something really the divine essence is predicated in itself. It is impossible for things really identical to be intuitively or abstractively known distinctly and their identity doubted. If any proposition is self-evident, it is one predicating the really same of the really same. The essence is really identical with whatever is really God, so no such proposition is doubtable or demonstrable.
claims: Nothing intrinsic to God can be demonstrated of the divine essence known in itself.
Propositions predicating the really same of the really same are most self-evident.
Distinctly known real identities cannot be doubted.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e2200.summary: Second argument: whatever is demonstrated of something is predicated first of that through which it is demonstrated, but nothing really identical with God can be predicated of anything before the divine essence, since there is nothing such (continued in the next paragraph).
claims: What is demonstrated of a subject is predicated first of the middle.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e2209.summary: Completing the argument: there is nothing except a person or relation, as will be shown. Against 'the Father is paternity; the essence is the Father; so the essence is paternity' as a demonstration: if this were doubtable for an intellect apprehending essence and paternity in themselves and could be made known by these premises, it would be demonstration, but no such intellect could doubt it. Against 'then it would be self-evident to every intellect and so to us': the proposition such an intellect forms is self-evident to anyone able to form it, but we cannot form it or its terms in this state. Our propositions under the common law have as terms concepts common to believers and unbelievers that supposit for essence and paternity, not for themselves. As the terms differ, so do the propositions, so one can be self-evident and the other doubtable and perhaps demonstrable. Even our 'God is God' is doubtable, being equivalent to 'the highest infinite being is the highest infinite being', which is false by false implication if the union of the subject's parts is false, as 'a white man is a white man' if no man is white. Second conclusion: nothing such can be demonstrated of a divine person, because of its real identity with whatever is predicated of it, so no such proposition can be doubtful to one who has it.
claims: An intellect knowing essence and paternity in themselves could not doubt their identity.
Our propositions about God have common concepts as terms that supposit for God.
Distinct terms make distinct propositions, so one can be self-evident and the other doubtable.
'God is God', as we form it, is doubtable.
Composite subjects carry an implication whose falsity makes the proposition false.
Nothing really identical with a divine person can be demonstrated of it.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e2309.summary: Answers the objection that such a proposition, though not doubtable to one knowing its terms distinctly and intuitively, could be doubtable to one knowing them confusedly and abstractively. It cannot be doubtful to anyone who has those terms, abstractively or intuitively, because the divine essence, being supremely simple, is necessarily known distinctly whenever it is known. Something confused, not the essence itself but predicable of it for the essence, can be known, but then a different thing is known and it is a different term. This holds for every simple created thing too, when it alone is known. Ockham says it on one opinion while also holding the other probable.
claims: The divine essence, being supremely simple, can only be known distinctly.
A confused concept predicable of God is a different term from the essence itself.
Every simple thing, known alone, is known distinctly.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e2357.summary: Concludes: the terms of such a proposition can only be known distinctly when no other terms are known, so a proposition with these terms and no others cannot be doubtful to any intellect. It is self-evident, a principle, and in no way a conclusion.
claims: Propositions with the divine essence and its intrinsic perfections as terms are self-evident principles.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e2374.summary: Third conclusion: common concepts predicated in quid of God and creatures cannot be demonstrated a priori of the divine essence in itself, nor of a simple proper concept of it if one is possible. Each such predication is immediate, since every common concept is immediately predicated of each item in its first division, and each such concept is immediately divided into God and creature: wisdom, intellect and goodness are each created or uncreated.
claims: Common quidditative concepts cannot be demonstrated a priori of God.
A common concept is immediately predicated of the members of its first division.
Wisdom, intellect and goodness are first divided into created and uncreated.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e2403.summary: Against 'every being is good; God is a being; so God is good' as a demonstration: taking 'good' as predicated in quid of God, it is not, since then 'good' and 'being' are simply synonymous. Taking 'good' as connoting something determinate, since it is the same as 'willable' and connotes will, it is in a way an a priori demonstration, but then it is not predicated of God in quid.
claims: 'Good' predicated in quid is synonymous with 'being'.
'Good' as connoting will ('willable') can be demonstrated of God in a way a priori.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e2423.summary: Fourth conclusion: connotative and negative concepts common to God and creatures can be demonstrated of the divine essence, if any are doubtable of the essence known in itself. Whatever is adequately predicable of a common term can be demonstrated of each item under it through that common term as middle. Such concepts are predicated first and adequately of something common to God and creatures, so they can be demonstrated through it. So perhaps 'every being is good; God is a being; so God is good' is a demonstration and in a way a priori.
claims: Common connotative and negative concepts can be demonstrated of God through a common middle.
What is adequately predicable of a common term is demonstrable of each item under it.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e2452.summary: That such a syllogism yields strict science and is a demonstration: it produces a truth-bearing habit that is not understanding, wisdom, and so on, so it is science.
claims: Such a syllogism yields science by elimination of other habits.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e2463.summary: Confirmation: this is no less a demonstration than a syllogism from simply posterior premises, which is granted to be a demonstration though not potissima, so all the more is this one.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e2481.summary: Fifth conclusion: connotative and negative concepts proper to God ('creative', 'omnipotent', 'eternal', 'infinite', 'immortal') are not demonstrable a priori of the divine essence in itself. Every a priori demonstration is through a middle to which the predicate belongs before the subject. Nothing can have such predicates before God: no real thing (nothing else can create), and no concept (what is proper to a thing belongs to it before any concept).
claims: Concepts proper to God, like 'creative' and 'omnipotent', are not demonstrable a priori of the divine essence.
A priori demonstration requires a middle to which the predicate belongs first.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e2515.summary: Answers the objection that such concepts can be demonstrated through their definitions ('whatever produces something from nothing is creative; God produces something from nothing; so God is creative'). This is not simple a priori demonstration, nor is any syllogism through definitions expressing only quid nominis. Simple a priori demonstration presupposes the nominal definition of all terms, and given that, one cannot know the premise predicating the definition while doubting the conclusion. Arguing from definition to defined is begging the question. Sixth conclusion: everything predicable of God in himself that is doubtable of our proper composite concept of God is demonstrable of that concept, through the divine essence in itself or a distinct cognition of deity as middle, or through something common. All such predicates belong first either to the essence (relations, notions, persons, proper negative and connotative concepts) or to something common to God and creatures (being, one, good, true). Sometimes one syllogism suffices, sometimes prosyllogisms are needed. Example: a non-blessed person can doubt 'God exists'. If God caused in them abstractive knowledge of the deity, they could demonstrate it: 'the divine essence exists; God is the divine essence; so God exists'. Those premises are not possible for us, only for an intellect knowing deity in itself. Only to such an intellect are these conclusions, which cannot be demonstrated through a common middle, demonstrable a priori.
claims: Syllogisms through nominal definitions are not simple demonstrations; they beg the question.
Predicates doubtable of our composite concept of God are demonstrable of it through the essence known in itself or a common middle.
An intellect with abstractive knowledge of deity could demonstrate 'God exists'.
Such premises are not available to us in this state.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e2643.summary: Raises further doubts. First: nothing seems demonstrable of God, since nothing belonging to God can belong first to something else, or something would be prior to God, so there is no middle.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e2659.summary: Second doubt: whether there can be several concepts of God. It seems so despite divine simplicity, since being, one, true and good are distinct concepts but not distinct beings, and definition and defined are distinct concepts of the same thing.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e2675.summary: Answers the first argument for the second opinion: attributive concepts, meaning simply absolute ones as opposed to connotative and negative, are not demonstrable of the divine essence, for the reason of the third conclusion. Against the claimed order: simple a priori demonstration requires an order of superior and inferior, whole and part, subject and accident, or a definition expressing real parts. Examples: the triangle's property shown of the isosceles; susceptibility to learning through the intellective soul; calefaction through heat; the angle-sum through 'figure contained by three lines'. The second and third reduce to demonstrations in oblique terms. Among the divine concepts there is no such order, because of divine simplicity. Against the principle that whatever order things would have if really distinct, they have by reason when distinct by reason while really one: on the common reading, that proposition is impossible by false implication, implying that things really one can be distinct by reason.
claims: Absolute attribute concepts are not demonstrable of God.
Simple a priori demonstration requires an order of superior/inferior, whole/part, subject/accident, or definition by real parts.
Divine concepts lack such an order because of divine simplicity.
Being really one yet distinct by reason implies a contradiction (on the common understanding).

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e2786.summary: Also false on another reading, that concepts corresponding to things that would be ordered if distinct have that order: things and their concepts are not always ordered alike. Man and whiteness are subject and accident, but their concepts are not so ordered. If man and animal were really distinct they would be potency and act, neither predicable of the other in the first mode, though now their concepts are related by first-mode predication. The same holds for being and God, and for God and deity, which if really distinct would be more and less perfect and not predicable of each other. So the order of concepts must be taken from the actual or possible order of things, not from an impossible supposition. Among things there is no order of superior and inferior, though among concepts there is (body, animal, man, this man).
claims: Things and their concepts are not always ordered alike.
The order of concepts should not be inferred from impossible suppositions about things.
There is no order of superior and inferior among things, only among concepts.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e2873.summary: Answers the minor premise: in that impossible case, perfect intellectual nature and perfect intellect would be related as subject and accident, but since the supposition includes a contradiction, the concepts need not now have such an order or provide a middle. If God and deity were really distinct, one would be part or subject of the other and could be a middle, but in fact it is not so.
claims: Orders under impossible suppositions do not carry over to the actual concepts.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e2898.summary: Against 'every intellectual nature is volitional; the divine essence is an intellectual nature; so it is volitional' as a priori demonstration: taking 'volitional' as a simply absolute concept, not connotative, it is not, since the immediate proposition is 'the divine nature is volitional', not 'every intellectual nature is volitional'. Taking 'volitional' as connotative, meaning 'able to have an act of willing', it can be demonstrated, as in the fourth conclusion.
claims: Absolute 'volitional' is predicated immediately of the divine nature.
Connotative 'volitional' can be demonstrated of God.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e2927.summary: Likewise for the personal notions: they lack an order sufficient for demonstration, though perhaps they would have one if really distinct. Even if really distinct, unless they had one of the orders listed, neither could be a middle for the other, just as whiteness and sweetness, even if one caused the other, could not serve as middle in universal demonstration.
claims: Even a causal order does not suffice for universal demonstration without one of the required orders.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e2953.summary: Answers the objection from Posterior Analytics II that any cause can be a middle: not in universal demonstration, as to universality of supposita and of times, as another question explains.
claims: Not every cause can be the middle of universal demonstration.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e2964.summary: Answers the argument from opposite orders: there is no such contrary order in demonstrations quia and propter quid as they imagine, since the same thing is concluded in both through different middles. Similarly to the third point: if divine nature, intellect and will were really distinct, omnipotence could be demonstrated of the essence through intellect and will, but there is no such order among these concepts now. Otherwise omnipotence would belong first to intellect or will, whereas it belongs first to the divine essence, since what belongs first and precisely to one thing can belong first only to it. So 'the divine essence is omnipotent' is immediate. This shows the falsity of the principle about real order, given the many counter-instances: not every act of understanding is the divine essence, and the concepts of animal and man are ordered as superior and inferior though the corresponding things are not.
claims: Quia and propter quid demonstrations conclude the same through different middles.
Omnipotence belongs first and immediately to the divine essence.
'The divine essence is omnipotent' is an immediate proposition.
The principle that conceptual order mirrors hypothetical real order is false.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e3038.summary: Answers the last argument for that opinion: there can be strict science of a simple thing without a definition, since it can be the subject of an accident that serves as middle. If a simple thing were constituted of formally distinct items, something might be demonstrated of it through one constituent ('the divine essence is creative; the Father is the divine essence; so the Father is creative'). Something can be demonstrated of a simple thing through a common middle, but nothing through its definition. Not any order of concepts suffices for science; it must be superior/inferior, part/whole, constituent/constituted, subject/accident, or definition/defined. So even if the concepts of intellect and will in God had some order, neither could be a middle for the other, as if in creatures intellect and will were really distinct powers each immediately perfecting the intellectual nature.
claims: There can be strict science of a simple thing without a definition.
'The Father is creative' may be demonstrated through the divine essence.
Not any order of concepts suffices for science.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e3099.summary: Answers 'everything intellective is volitional; the rational soul is intellective; so it is volitional': whether or not it is propter quid, it is not simple a priori demonstration, because intellect is not prior to will as its subject. Will belongs first to the nature, which is both intellectual and volitional.
claims: Will does not belong to intellect as its subject but to the intellectual nature.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e3120.summary: Answers 'every demonstration through what is prior is a priori': not any priority suffices; priority of subject is required.
claims: A priori demonstration requires priority of subject.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e3129.summary: Answers 'sometimes there is a priori demonstration through an extrinsic cause': such demonstration is not universal as to times and supposita, as another question explains.
claims: Demonstrations through extrinsic causes are not universal as to times and supposita.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e3145.summary: Answers the first doubt: something can be demonstrated of God. Ockham grants that something is prior to God by priority of predication, and such a prior item must be the middle in demonstrating something of God.
claims: Something is prior to God in priority of predication.
Common concepts prior by predication serve as middles in demonstrations about God.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e3156.summary: Answers the second doubt: there can be distinct concepts only through some distinction in reality, of things in the same thing, of wholly disparate things, or of formally distinct items. There would be no distinct concepts of God unless God were distinct from created wisdom, created will, intellection and volition, and this distinction suffices. So all such concepts are common and univocal to God and creatures, or to some creature, or follow on them. 'One', 'true', 'good' consequently import distinct things: 'true' connotes understanding and 'good' willing, and without connoting really distinct things they would not be distinct concepts. Superior and inferior concepts differ because one imports more things than the other, and definition and defined differ through the things the definition imports.
claims: Distinct concepts require some distinction in reality.
Concepts predicated of God are univocal to God and creatures or follow on such concepts.
'True' connotes understanding and 'good' connotes willing.
Superior concepts import more things than inferior ones.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e3200.summary: Answers the first opinion's first argument: 'to know is through a cause' does not mean precisely an incomplex real cause properly speaking, but anything to which something demonstrable belongs first. That is a cause in an extended sense, since it follows formally that if it does not belong to this, it does not belong to others, and not the reverse. Even if Aristotle gives a proper definition there, he extends 'cause' to every first subject of a demonstrable predicate, which is compatible with its being a true definition. The subject of a science need not be caused, composite, or have a really different property or a definition, to be discussed later.
claims: 'Cause' in Aristotle's definition of knowledge extends to whatever a demonstrable predicate belongs to first.
The subject of a science need not be caused, composite, or have a really distinct property.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e3235.summary: Answers the first principal argument: what is demonstrable need not have a cause properly speaking. It suffices that there be something prior to which it belongs first, at least in predication.
claims: Demonstrability requires only something prior in predication.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e3245.summary: Answers the second: not every demonstration has a definition as middle.
claims: Not every demonstration has a definition as middle.

wo8uy7-d1e81-d1e3252.summary: Answers the third: something is predicated of God in the second mode of per se predication, and God has properties, as will be shown, but they need not differ really from him.
claims: Something is predicated of God per se in the second mode.
God has properties that do not differ really from him.

wo8uy7-d1e81.summary: Prologue question 2 asks whether evident knowledge of theological truths, granted possible by divine power, is scientia proprie dicta. Ockham first defines the strictly knowable proposition: necessary, doubtable, and apt to be made evident by syllogism from evident necessary premises. This excludes contingent, self-evident, and experiential first principles such as 'heat is calefactive'. He defends dubitability against objections, conceding that God lacks science in this strict sense, and develops an account of experiential knowledge. Some arts resolve to self-evident principles (Augustine's anamnesis), others to principles grasped through sense, memory and experience (Aristotle). A single experiment with other causes excluded, together with the principle that like individuals have like effects, yields universal principles for a most specific species, while genera require induction over species. Knowledge from experience and from demonstration are of the same species. Science is evident knowledge of a necessary truth apt to be caused by syllogistic discourse. He rejects the view that knowledge of God cannot be science for lack of real causes, and attacks Scotus's view that divine attributes, notionals and relations ad extra are demonstrable propter quid through an order of rationes. No real or rational distinction grounds quidditative versus denominative concepts in God; formal distinction would not help; and concepts do not mirror the order things would have if really distinct. His own conclusions: nothing intrinsic to God is demonstrable of the divine essence or a person known in itself, since such propositions are self-evident. Our propositions about God use common concepts and so can be doubtable. Common quidditative concepts are not demonstrable a priori of God; common connotative and negative ones are (through being as middle); proper connotative ones like 'creative' are not. Predicates doubtable of our composite concept of God are demonstrable through the essence known in itself or a common middle, though only an intellect knowing deity could do so. Distinct concepts of God require connotation of distinct creaturely things.
claims: A strictly knowable proposition is necessary, doubtable, and syllogistically evidenced.
God lacks science in the strict, discursive sense.
Experience plus the uniformity principle yields evident universal principles.
Nothing intrinsic to God is demonstrable of the divine essence known in itself.
Common connotative and negative concepts can be demonstrated of God through common middles.
Concepts proper to God like 'creative' are not demonstrable a priori.
Distinct concepts of God require connotation of distinct things.
